children: Executives at iron ore majors BHP
are due to meet with China's premier and business leaders in Beijing on Friday, as Australia's top trade partner ramps up pressure on producers of the country's most valuable export.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and 11 high-level executives, including Rio Tinto's head of iron ore Matt Holcz and BHP's Australia boss Geraldine Slattery, will meet Chinese Premier Li Qiang and Chinese company executives for a CEO roundtable, according to the Business Council of Australia, an industry association.

The meeting comes amid increasingly fraught negotiations between Australia's top miners and China's state iron ore buyer, China Mineral Resources Group, as centralisation of its buying increases the country's bargaining power in negotiating contracts.
CMRG banned steelmakers from buying specific products from BHP, Fortescue
and Rio Tinto while annual supply negotiations were underway this year, a practice that has stirred increasing concern in Canberra.
Australia's Resources Minister Madeleine King said this week that any potential manipulation of trade in iron ore would be against international rules and a threat to government revenues.
Australia's iron ore exports are expected to reap A$107 billion ($72.16 billion) in the current financial year, according to government estimates.

Goldman Sachs expects CMRG's influence over iron ore prices to increase in coming years, it said in a research note on Saturday. Goldman analysts cut their EBITDA forecasts for listed Australian miners by up to $9 billion over the next decade, assuming a price range of $85 to $90 per metric ton. Prices of iron ore on the Singapore Exchange slipped below $90 a ton to the lowest in four years this week.

CMRG has reached new supply deals with BHP and Rio Tinto this year. Fortescue, however, has warned its operations could be affected if talks with the state-backed buyer do not conclude by year-end. The Business Council of Australia did not list any Fortescue executives as attending the roundtable on Friday.

Although some iron ore miners have sought Canberra's help in the price fight, investors and analysts said Australia's government has been trying to repair its relationship with China and it might not want to take up this fight right now.
China imposed unofficial bans on a range of Australian commodity exports, including coal, wine and beef, between 2020 and 2023.
